title: How does ZGC achieve sub-millisecond pauses (colored pointers, load barriers, concurrent relocation, self-healing references), and what is Generational ZGC (Java 21 opt-in → 23 default → 24 exclusive via JEP 490)?
shortTitle: How ZGC achieves sub-millisecond pauses — colored pointers, load barriers, concurrent relocation, self-healing references — and what Generational ZGC is

s1_definition.profdef: ZGC is a scalable, low-latency, mostly-concurrent garbage collector whose stop-the-world pauses stay under a millisecond regardless of heap size. It achieves this by doing marking and relocation concurrently with the application, using colored pointers to store GC metadata in the reference bits and load barriers that fix up references lazily when the application reads them. Generational ZGC, opt-in in Java 21, default in Java 23, and the only mode in Java 24 via JEP 490, splits the heap into young and old generations so most collection effort targets the short-lived young objects.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine renovating the bank while customers keep transacting. Instead of locking the whole branch for hours, the crew moves one desk at a time in the background. They tag each file with a coloured sticker that says "this file is being moved." When a teller picks up a file and sees the sticker, the teller instantly updates their note to the new location and carries on — nobody waits for the whole renovation to finish. The coloured stickers are colored pointers, the teller's instant update is the load barrier and self-healing, and the one-desk-at-a-time move is concurrent relocation.
s1_definition.oneliner: ZGC keeps pauses under a millisecond by marking and moving objects concurrently, using colored pointers plus load barriers so references self-heal to the new location on first read.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** ZGC is a scalable, low-latency, mostly-concurrent garbage collector whose stop-the-world pauses stay under a millisecond regardless of heap size. It achieves this by doing marking and relocation concurrently with the application, using colored pointers to store GC metadata in the reference bits and load barriers that fix up references lazily when the application reads them. Generational ZGC, opt-in in Java 21, default in Java 23, and the only mode in Java 24 via JEP 490, splits the heap into young and old generations so most collection effort targets the short-lived young objects.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine renovating the bank while customers keep transacting. Instead of locking the whole branch for hours, the crew moves one desk at a time in the background. They tag each file with a coloured sticker that says "this file is being moved." When a teller picks up a file and sees the sticker, the teller instantly updates their note to the new location and carries on — nobody waits for the whole renovation to finish. The coloured stickers are colored pointers, the teller's instant update is the load barrier and self-healing, and the one-desk-at-a-time move is concurrent relocation.

**One line to remember:** ZGC keeps pauses under a millisecond by marking and moving objects concurrently, using colored pointers plus load barriers so references self-heal to the new location on first read.

sections.s2_technical:
The core trick is colored pointers. On a sixty-four-bit JVM a heap reference does not need all its bits for the address, so ZGC steals a few bits to store GC state such as Marked, Remapped, and (in generational mode) which generation. The address bits still point at the object; the colour bits tell ZGC what phase-relevant work, if any, is pending for that reference.

Load barriers are small snippets of code the JIT inserts on every reference load. When the application reads a reference, the barrier checks the colour bits. If the colour is already current, it is nearly free and the read proceeds. If the colour is stale — for example the object has been relocated — the barrier does the fix-up right then: it looks up the object's new address and rewrites the reference in place. This is self-healing: the reference is corrected on first touch, so each reference is fixed at most once per cycle and the cost is spread across the application rather than paid in one giant pause.

Concurrent relocation means ZGC compacts the heap while the application runs. It selects regions (ZGC calls them "pages") that are mostly garbage, copies the few live objects out to fresh pages, and lets the load barriers lazily repoint any references that still point at the old location. The actual stop-the-world pauses are tiny and bounded — only short root-scanning and handshake steps — which is why pause time does not grow with heap size. ZGC scales to multi-terabyte heaps with the same sub-millisecond pauses.

Generational ZGC adds a young and an old generation on top of this machinery. The weak generational hypothesis says most objects die young, so collecting the young generation frequently and cheaply reclaims most garbage for far less work than scanning the whole heap every time. Non-generational ZGC marked the entire heap on every cycle, which wasted effort and needed more headroom. Generational ZGC was opt-in in Java 21 with `-XX:+ZGenerational`, became the default in Java 23, and in Java 24 JEP 490 removed the non-generational mode entirely so ZGC is always generational.

You enable ZGC with `-XX:+UseZGC`. On Java 21 and 22 add `-XX:+ZGenerational` for the generational mode; from Java 23 onward it is already generational. ZGC is the right choice when you need consistent low latency on a large heap and can afford a little extra CPU and memory headroom for the concurrent work.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a real-time fraud-scoring service that holds a large in-memory graph of recent transactions, several gigabytes, and must respond to the payment switch within a strict latency budget. With a stop-the-world collector, the occasional long pause blows the budget and causes false timeouts. This is exactly what ZGC solves — pauses stay sub-millisecond even on a multi-gigabyte heap.

Problem 2 — Most scoring objects are short-lived request context, but the transaction graph lives for hours. Marking the whole heap every cycle just to reclaim the short-lived junk is wasteful. This is exactly what Generational ZGC solves — collect the young generation often and cheaply, leave the long-lived graph mostly untouched.

Our mini-project is a runnable demo that builds a long-lived graph and churns many short-lived scoring contexts, logs heap usage and GC behaviour, and prints the correct ZGC flags for Java 21 versus Java 23 and later. Classes are `FraudScoringSimulator` (driver), `TransactionGraph` (long-lived old-gen resident), `ScoringContext` (short-lived young-gen churn), and `GcObserver` (reads garbage-collector beans and logs counts and times).
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
zgc-fraud-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── run.sh
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/zgc/
            ├── FraudScoringSimulator.java   (main + demo classes)
            └── GcObserver.java
```

Configuration (JVM flags):

```bash
# zgc-flags.conf
# Java 21/22 — generational is opt-in
-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xms4g -Xmx4g
# Java 23+ — ZGC is generational by default
-XX:+UseZGC -Xms4g -Xmx4g
# Low-latency hardening (see container question)
-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn -q clean package

# Java 23+: ZGC is generational by default
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,tags \
     -cp target/zgc-fraud-demo-1.0.0.jar com.bank.jvm.zgc.FraudScoringSimulator

# Java 21/22: add the opt-in flag
java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xms4g -Xmx4g \
     -cp target/zgc-fraud-demo-1.0.0.jar com.bank.jvm.zgc.FraudScoringSimulator

# Confirm pauses are tiny
grep -i "Pause" gc.log | head
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a long-lived `TransactionGraph` of two hundred thousand nodes and five million short-lived `ScoringContext` objects, each referencing the graph.

Step 1. The graph is built once. After a couple of young collections it is promoted into the old generation, where it stays. Its references carry colour bits that ZGC will update lazily if it ever relocates the graph.

Step 2. The loop creates one `ScoringContext` per iteration with a thirty-two-element feature array. These are young-generation objects that die almost immediately after `score()` runs.

Step 3. When the application reads the `graph` reference inside `score()`, the JIT-inserted load barrier checks the colour bits. If ZGC has relocated the graph in the background, the barrier transparently repoints the reference to the new address and rewrites it in place — this is self-healing, and the application does not stall.

Step 4. The young generation fills. ZGC performs a concurrent young collection: it marks live young objects and relocates survivors to fresh pages while the loop keeps running. The stop-the-world portion is a tiny handshake, well under a millisecond.

Step 5. The large old-generation graph is collected far less often. Because generational ZGC focuses effort on the young generation, it does not re-scan the whole heap every cycle, so the long-lived graph incurs almost no ongoing GC cost.

Step 6. `GcObserver` logs the collection count and total pause milliseconds. Even after five million allocations, the total pause time stays small and the per-pause time stays sub-millisecond, which the gc.log confirms.


sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Allocation: 200,000-node graph (long-lived) + 5,000,000 contexts (short-lived)
    │
    ▼
  Young generation (ScoringContext churn)
    │ fills fast
    ▼
  Concurrent Young Collection
    │ mark (concurrent) → relocate survivors (concurrent)
    │ STW = tiny handshake (< 1 ms)
    ▼
  app reads graph reference
    │ Load Barrier checks colour bits
    ├─ colour current ─→ nearly free, proceed
    └─ colour stale   ─→ self-heal: repoint to new address, rewrite in place
    ▼
  Old generation (TransactionGraph)
    │ collected rarely (generational focus on young)
    ▼
  Sub-ms pauses regardless of 4GB heap
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
ZGC is a low-latency, mostly-concurrent collector whose stop-the-world pauses stay under a millisecond no matter how large the heap is, scaling from a few gigabytes to multiple terabytes with the same tiny pauses. It achieves this by doing the expensive work — marking and relocation — concurrently with the running application, and by using two clever mechanisms. The first is colored pointers: on a sixty-four-bit machine the reference has spare bits, so ZGC stores GC metadata like Marked and Remapped directly in those bits. The second is load barriers, small pieces of code the JIT inserts on every reference read; when the application loads a reference the barrier checks the colour, and if the object has been relocated it transparently repoints the reference to the new address right then. That is self-healing — each reference is corrected at most once per cycle, on first touch, so the cost is spread smoothly instead of being paid in one long pause.

Because relocation happens concurrently and references fix themselves lazily, the only stop-the-world work left is short root scanning and handshakes, which is why pause time is independent of heap size. That is the headline property that makes ZGC the right choice for large-heap, latency-critical services.

Generational ZGC adds young and old generations on top of this. Since most objects die young, collecting the young generation frequently and cheaply reclaims the bulk of garbage without re-scanning the whole heap every cycle, which the old non-generational mode had to do. It was opt-in in Java 21 with the ZGenerational flag, became the default in Java 23, and in Java 24 JEP 490 removed the non-generational mode so ZGC is now always generational. At National Bank of India I used it for a real-time fraud-scoring service that held a multi-gigabyte transaction graph in memory and had to answer the payment switch inside a tight budget; ZGC kept the ninety-ninth-percentile pause sub-millisecond while the generational young collections absorbed the heavy churn of short-lived scoring contexts, and I watched the allocation-stall count and pause percentile on the dashboard to prove it stayed within budget.
